transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-14
Time: 15:00–15:54 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Marcus (CTO Umbrage), Priya (ML Eng), Daniel (Infra)

Summary:
Short intake focused on per-token economics, batching and KV/prefix caching levers, and routing between hosted / dedicated / private footprints. Customer has a constrained pilot budget and strong latency SLAs for a fraud-detection scoring feature. They want a predictable spend ceiling and a fallback routing plan if dedicated capacity is saturated.

Topics:
- Current latency targets and QPS profile
- Per-token pricing expectations and budget caps
- Batching window tradeoffs and prefix/KV cache reuse
- Dedicated vs hosted routing and automatic fallbacks
- Security (VPC, KMS) and SOC2 docs requested

--- Transcript body ---
00:00 Sofia: All right everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intro — i'm Sofia from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, and Liam our SE will go deep on the cost model. Marcus?
00:12 Marcus: Hey all, Marcus here. We're trying to scope a pilot for a high-throughput fraud scoring endpoint. We have budgetary constraints so we wanted to understand how to keep per-score costs under, uh, a hard ceiling.
00:25 Priya: and to add, our expected payloads are short, like 60-120 tokens typically, sometimes longer with context. Latency target is 120ms p95.
00:34 Liam: okay great. So two levers we'll talk about: first is the per-token runtime cost — which varies by model + quantization + batching; second is caching and routing — prefix/KV cache to avoid repeated compute for repeated contexts.
00:48 Daniel: quick question — are you able to route to a cheaper model automatically if we're hitting budget caps? Like fallback to a smaller quantized variant?
00:55 Liam: yes — we support smart routing policies. You can define rules: prefer dedicated for latency-critical requests, fall back to hosted cheaper variants when dedicated is saturated or budget thresholds are reached. We do automatic compatibility checks for model variants so you don't get format regressions.
01:13 Marcus: can you explain how batching affects latency? Our app can't queue for very long.
01:18 Liam: totally — batching improves tokens/sec but increases tail latency because you wait for the batch window. With our runtime you can set max batch window in ms, and priority/latency lanes. For example for 120ms p95 we usually set very small batch windows (like 10-30ms) and aggressive continuous batching for small groups; that reduces cost but only modestly if QPS is low.
01:36 Priya: what's the unit economics delta between small batch windows and no batching?
01:40 Liam: depends a lot on model and QPS. For a 7B-class model quantized to int8, we typically see 20-35% cost improvement with small batching windows at medium QPS; with large windows 40-60%. For 70B models differences are larger. But small windows are the practical tradeoff for your latency needs.
01:58 Sofia: to make this concrete, we'll send a pilot pricing worksheet with modeled scenarios: hosted-only, dedicated-only reserved for your peak QPS, and a hybrid routing approach with automatic fallbacks.
02:08 Marcus: about caching — our traffic has a lot of repeat prefixes for user metadata. How much can prefix/KV cache actually save?
02:17 Liam: prefix caching can be huge if the same prefix shows up often. For NLU-style repeats we often see 30-70% token compute savings because you skip the repeated prefix tokens entirely and only compute on the new tokens. KV cache is more for multi-turn chat but the idea is the same. We also do partial-merge caching so you don't need perfect matches.
02:33 Daniel: what's the cache residency in your hosted environment? Do we control TTLs?
02:37 Liam: on Hosted we manage cache nodes but you can set TTLs and pin certain prefixes. On Private/Dedicated you control everything and can keep longer residency. For pilot we can show both numbers.
02:46 Priya: any gotchas? Like are there cases where the cache actually increases cost due to cache misses?
02:51 Liam: good point — if you have very high diversity of prompts, caching helps less. Also there's some memory and warm-up overhead in certain workloads. We'll model that in the benchmark.
03:03 Marcus: pricing — your public per-token numbers are one thing, but we need a committed monthly cap. Can we do a rate-limited committed pool?
03:10 Sofia: yes, for Dedicated we do reserved capacity with monthly commits, and we can put in throttles and burst policies. For hosted pilots we can set budget alerts and a safety fallback: when spend hits X% we can route non-critical traffic to cheaper models or reduce max generation lengths.
03:26 Marcus: can that be automated? We don't want a manual toggle in the middle of an incident.
03:30 Liam: absolutely — you can define automated policies: e.g., if monthly burn rate exceeds threshold, redirect requests with tag "best-effort" to smaller quantized variants or to inference cache-only path. We also expose per-token counters so you can do custom logic.
03:44 Priya: how precise are the per-token counters? We need to map to our internal cost allocation per feature.
03:48 Sofia: token billing aligns with model-token output and includes prompt + completion. We give token breakdown per route, per model, per API key. Liam: and you can tag requests so the console breaks down cost by feature.
03:59 Daniel: security wise — we need VPC peering and customer-managed KMS for Private. Does Redwood allow on-prem private deployments?
04:06 Liam: yes, Private deployments support VPC-only control plane and you can bring your KMS / HSM. There's an on-prem appliance option if you need air-gap. SOC2 docs we can share after the call.
04:18 Marcus: benchmark run — we want realistic numbers. We'll supply a prompt set and expected QPS distribution. Can you run it on dedicated GPUs and show cost per 10k decisions?
04:27 Liam: yes. For the benchmark we'll run on a dedicated pool matching your instance types; we'll include runs with int8 quantization and a float16 baseline. We'll also run a hosted run to compare.
04:37 Priya: what about inference kernels — do you rely on vendor-specific libs? We have concerns about model fidelity when quantized.
04:43 Liam: we use model-aware kernel selection and compare output quality in the eval harness. For critical features we recommend a quality gate: run evals on a holdout set and compare distributions (exact-match, similarity metrics). Quantization sometimes changes outputs subtly; we'll show quality delta alongside cost numbers.
04:58 Marcus: what's the timeline if we wanted to start pilot in two weeks?
05:01 Sofia: doable. Typical pilot steps: 1) share prompt set + QPS profile, 2) Redwood builds benchmark and pricing scenarios (2-4 days), 3) run pilot on small dedicated pool or hosted hybrid (1-2 weeks), 4) iterate and finalize SOW.
05:14 Daniel: okay. Another question — burst capacity. If dedicated pool is at capacity, can we overflow to hosted in the same request path?
05:21 Liam: yes — that's the fallback policy I mentioned. You can have primary route to dedicated low-latency pool and overflow to hosted. There's a small added routing latency but it's minimal — usually single-digit ms. You can also define per-route token-thresholds to keep within budget.
05:33 Priya: how do we handle model version pinning? We need reproducibility for analysis.
05:36 Sofia: you can pin model versions in the deployment config; rollouts support canary and A/B. We'll keep history logs and trace tokens per model id.
05:43 Marcus: what day-to-day visibility will we have during pilot for burn and latency?
05:47 Sofia: Console gives token-level burn by API key, latency heatmaps, and per-route SLO dashboards. We also provide a weekly summary and can open a slack channel for incident alerts.
05:57 Liam: to add, we can export traces to your tracing system; we include sampling hooks so you can reconstruct problematic requests.
06:06 Marcus: are there any licensing minimums or hidden fees for Private?
06:09 Sofia: Private has a platform fee plus support tier; we'll put numbers in the pilot worksheet. No surprise hidden fees — network egress is passed through where applicable.
06:18 Priya: can you do token-slicing — like limit max gen length at runtime per route?
06:22 Liam: yes — runtime supports max tokens per request and we also offer transforms to truncate or rewrite prompts at the gateway to optimize costs.
06:30 Daniel: regarding quota enforcement — if we hit budget cap and redirect, will client receives 200 with truncated response or 429?
06:36 Liam: depends on your policy. Options are: 1) return 429, 2) return 200 with lower-cost model output and a header flag, or 3) queue briefly (not ideal). Many customers prefer option 2 for graceful degradation.
06:48 Marcus: ok good.
06:50 [silence, notes exchanged]
07:10 Priya: i have a niche question: for short inference paths (single-turn scoring) is kv cache relevant? Feels like waste.
07:16 Liam: right — KV cache shines for multi-turn or repeated prefix sets. For pure single-turn stateless scoring probably less helpful; caching at the feature level (memoization) might be better.
07:26 Marcus: you mentioned automated budget routing earlier — can we set different policies by tenant? We have multi-tenant product and want stricter limits for free-tier tenants.
07:35 Sofia: yes — per-API-key or per-tenant labels let you route differently. You can have free-tier hit hosted low-cost variants, pro hit dedicated, etc.
07:44 Daniel: one more about observability — do you expose raw token counts per request in logs?
07:48 Liam: yes we expose token counts and model id. We also provide aggregated counters and can export to your billing system.
08:00 [moderate side conversation about internal approvals at Umbrage]
08:50 Marcus: budget constraints — we want a hard monthly cap of $12k for pilot (not per feature, total). Can Redwood guarantee we won't exceed?
08:59 Sofia: we can set throttles and automated fallback rules but not absolute guarantees for hosted pilots because of shared infra. For Dedicated with a committed capacity, you get predictable throughput for your committed allotment. We can set hard throttles at the gateway too — any requests beyond are 429.
09:14 Marcus: if we do Dedicated, is there a minimum?
09:17 Sofia: there is a reserved capacity minimum for Dedicated pilots — typically a small pool (e.g., equivalent to 1-2 GPU nodes) with monthly commit. We'll include an option in the worksheet that fits your $12k cap.
09:28 Priya: will the committed capacity sit idle and cost us even if we don't use it?
09:32 Sofia: yes — reserved capacity is a commit. That's why many teams prefer hybrid: reserved for baseline, hosted overflow for spikes. That reduces wasted spend but gives some predictability.
09:41 Marcus: can you model a hybrid where baseline is reserved for x tokens/day and overflow to hosted at Y cost?
09:46 Liam: absolutely — we'll model expected token distribution, reserved baseline, overflow probability, and expected monthly burn. We'll produce a per-10k decisions metric so you can compare.
09:58 Marcus: about quality — if overflow goes to a quantized smaller model, will our fraud-detection decisions degrade?
10:03 Liam: likely some delta. That's why we recommend a quality gate: run A/B tests where a sample of overflow traffic is still sent to baseline to measure real-world regression, and automatic rollback if quality dips.
10:14 Priya: ok makes sense.
10:18 Daniel: operationally — who runs the benchmark and where will we host test data? We need to avoid PII leaving our environment.
10:24 Sofia: we can run the benchmark in your VPC via a private deployment if needed, or you can obfuscate the data before sharing. For early pilots many customers provide sanitized prompt sets.
10:36 Marcus: prefer VPC for pilot if possible.
10:39 Sofia: noted. We'll include a Private deployment option in the worksheet and add network diagram requirements.
10:45 [brief pause: notes being typed]
11:05 Liam: follow-up detail: batching windows are tunable per route, and there's a concept of latency lanes; you can commit to a lane in the route config. That lets you keep strict p95 while allowing other lanes to batch more aggressively.
11:18 Priya: do you provide examples of lane configs?
11:21 Liam: yes we'll share example configs and a sample JSON.
11:24 Marcus: what's the expected cost reduction from pinning a model to int8?
11:28 Liam: for your profile probably 25-45% at the cost of slight quality variance — we'll quantify on your prompts.
11:36 [crosstalk — minor interruption]
11:50 Priya: we also have a compliance review next week; can we get SOC2 and encryption docs before then?
11:55 Sofia: yes — i'll send SOC2 + encryption + network diagrams as one packet by the end of day tomorrow.
12:02 Marcus: perfect.
12:05 Sofia: quick recap of next steps then: 1) Umbrage shares sanitized prompt set, QPS profiles and the pilot budget cap ($12k). 2) Redwood sends pilot pricing worksheet + example lane configs + SOC2/network docs by 2026-01-16. 3) Redwood runs benchmark on dedicated and hosted (with int8 vs fp16) and returns cost per 10k decisions and quality deltas by 2026-01-20. 4) Follow up call to review in one week (tentatively 2026-01-21).
12:28 Marcus: that plan works. Any blockers on our side?
12:32 Daniel: just internal approval and sanitized data prep. We'll try to get the prompts to you by EOD Monday.
12:38 Sofia: great, we'll queue the benchmark as soon as we have the prompt set.
12:45 [wrap up pleasantries]
13:00 Sofia: thanks everyone — we'll send the worksheet and docs. Liam will follow up on the benchmark plan.
13:07 Marcus: thanks.
